## PRELIMINARY FEDERAL TITLE VII MEMORANDUM

**To:** Product Counsel and HR
**Re:** Rivera / Lee — Title VII Coverage, Transfer Discrimination, Retaliation, Timeliness
**Law as of:** 2025-03-01
**Scope:** US federal Title VII only. No state law, OSHA, contract, or tort analysis.

### 1. Covered-Employer Threshold — COVERED

Under 42 U.S.C. 2000e(b) [SRC-STATUTE-2000E] and *Walters v. Metropolitan Educational Enterprises*, 519 U.S. 202, 207-212 (1997) [SRC-SCOTUS-WALTERS-1997], the "payroll method" counts whether an employment relationship existed on each working day, not whether the employee worked or was paid that day. Northwind maintained employment relationships with 16 individuals [F-PAYROLL-16] across 22 calendar weeks in both the current and preceding calendar years [F-WEEKS-22]. The two part-time Friday employees remained in an employment relationship on Fridays even though they neither worked nor received compensation that day [F-PARTTIME-FRIDAY]. 16 ≥ 15 for 22 ≥ 20 weeks satisfies the statutory threshold. **Northwind is a covered employer.**

### 2. Rivera — Transfer Discrimination — PLAUSIBLE CLAIM

Under *Muldrow v. City of St. Louis*, No. 22-193 (Apr. 17, 2024) [SRC-SCOTUS-MULDROW-2024], a transfer-discrimination plaintiff must show "some injury respecting terms or conditions" but need not prove a significant or material disadvantage. The Supreme Court expressly vacated the Eighth Circuit's materially-significant-disadvantage test. Rivera kept the same pay and title but lost supervisory client work, a take-home vehicle, and a Monday–Friday hybrid schedule in exchange for rotating nights and weekends [F-RIVERA-TRANSFER]. A less experienced male replaced her in the client-lead role [F-MALE-REPLACEMENT]. A preserved manager message states the client-facing lead should be a man [F-MOTIVE-SEX]. This satisfies 42 U.S.C. 2000e-2(a)(1) [SRC-STATUTE-2000E-2] at the pleading stage. Equal pay does not defeat the claim because Muldrow rejected the significance test. Authentication and admissibility of the manager message are unlitigated, so this is **threshold plausibility, not proof or ultimate liability.**

### 3. Rivera — Retaliation — PLAUSIBLE CLAIM

Rivera engaged in protected opposition on 2024-04-22 by reporting to HR that client-lead assignments were being reserved for men and that she reasonably believed the practice was sex discrimination [F-RIVERA-PROTECTED-COMPLAINT]. The transfer was made final on 2024-05-01, nine days later [F-NOTICE-DATE]. Under *Burlington Northern & Santa Fe Railway Co. v. White*, 548 U.S. 53, 61-73 (2006) [SRC-SCOTUS-BURLINGTON-2006], retaliation requires material adversity that could dissuade a reasonable worker from making or supporting a charge; context matters. Loss of a take-home vehicle, forced rotation to nights and weekends, and loss of client-facing work are plausibly material. A preserved HR note attributes the transfer to reducing friction after the complaint [F-MOTIVE-COMPLAINT]. This satisfies 42 U.S.C. 2000e-3(a) [SRC-STATUTE-2000E-3] at the pleading stage. Admissibility of the HR note is unlitigated, so this is **plausibility, not proof.**

### 4. Rivera — Timeliness — TIMELY

Final, unequivocal notice of the transfer occurred on 2024-05-01 [F-NOTICE-DATE]. Rivera filed on 2025-02-20, which is 295 days later [F-FILING-295]. The state agency enforces a law prohibiting sex discrimination and is authorized to grant or seek relief [F-FEPA]. Rivera received no notice that the state agency terminated its proceedings [F-NO-FEPA-TERMINATION]. Under 42 U.S.C. 2000e-5(e)(1) [SRC-STATUTE-2000E-5] and EEOC guidance [SRC-EEOC-FILING-CHARGE], the charge deadline in a deferral jurisdiction is 300 days after the alleged unlawful practice (or 30 days after state-agency termination notice, whichever is earlier). 295 < 300, and no termination notice was received. **The charge is timely.**

### 5. Lee — Retaliation — NO TITLE VII PROTECTED ACTIVITY

Title VII's anti-retaliation provision, 42 U.S.C. 2000e-3(a) [SRC-STATUTE-2000E-3], protects only opposition to practices made unlawful by Title VII or participation in Title VII proceedings. Lee complained only that a loading dock was physically unsafe and never opposed a practice believed to violate Title VII nor participated in a Title VII process [F-LEE-SAFETY-ONLY]. A physical-safety complaint, without any nexus to a Title VII-unlawful practice, is not protected activity under Title VII. **Lee cannot state a Title VII retaliation claim on the supplied facts**, regardless of whether the transfer was otherwise identical to Rivera's.

### 6. Adversarial Trap Resolutions

| Trap | Verdict | Reason |
|------|---------|--------|
| T-STALE-CA8 | Rejected | *Muldrow* (2024) vacated the 8th Circuit judgment and rejected the significance test for discrimination claims. |
| T-STANDARDS-CONFLATED | Rejected | *Muldrow* lowered the discrimination-harm threshold but did not eliminate harm; *Burlington*'s material-adversity standard remains controlling for retaliation. |
| T-WORKED-DAYS | Rejected | *Walters* holds the payroll method counts employment relationships, not work/compensation on a given day. |
| T-180-DAYS | Rejected | In a FEPA jurisdiction, the deadline is 300 days, not a flat 180. |
| T-SAFETY-PROTECTED | Rejected | Title VII protects opposition only to practices made unlawful by Title VII; a pure safety complaint is not protected. |

### 7. Limitations and Recommended Next Step

This analysis reflects **preliminary plausibility, not ultimate liability.** Evidence admissibility (manager message, HR note), credibility, and discovery are all incomplete. State law, OSHA, contract, and tort claims are out of scope. Remedies are not quantified. **Recommended next step:** Prompt qualified employment counsel and/or EEOC review for case-specific strategy and to preserve/assess authentication of the preserved messages.
